label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here it is. I kept it in English (with a couple of French words slipping in, because that's how you'd actually write it) — hot but not hateful, and it ends with a clear ask so he can't pretend he didn't understand.

**Subject: The building on Saint-Hubert — please call me. Do not answer by text.**

---

Denis,

I'm writing this email instead of calling you, because every time I try to talk about this I end up half French, half insult, and I don't want to say things to you that I'll have to be sorry for later. So I'm writing it down. Please read all of it before you answer me.

I'm not going to start with the money. I'm going to start with Thursday.

---

**Thursday, 6 in the morning.** I was at the bench shaping baguettes. A man walks into my shop with a camera. He tells me he was sent by the agency to photograph the building, and that you told him I was okay with it. He said it to me like he was asking me for the wifi password. Then he walked through my bakery with his camera and shot the sign, the counter, the ovens, the staircase that goes up to the two apartments.

Karine had to calm me down. My hands were shaking on the dough and I could not keep it together. I have been running this bakery for thirty-one years and I have never, not once, lost control in the middle of a shift like that.

You didn't call me, Denis. You sent a photographer with a camera into my shop at six in the morning and told a stranger I was "ok with it." Do you understand what you did there? You didn't think of me. You didn't think that I'm the one standing in that building every single morning at four a.m. You figured the easiest thing was to make it look like I had agreed to something. That is not business. That's not even strategy. That is a coward's way, and I hate writing that word about my brother, but it is the word.

And then I remember what you said to me. After maman's funeral. You called me and you said, *"There's no rush, we decide together."*

**Together.**

I hung up that phone and I felt relieved. I went back into the kitchen and I told Karine, *at least we'll do it right, at least it'll be fair.* I waited for you. Weeks went by. I waited. Every time the phone rang I thought, it's him, he's finally going to call me about the building. And then I saw the listing on Centris.

$1,150,000. My father's building, with a floor plan and a brochure and photos of my own storefront with somebody else's watermark on them. I sat in my office and I read the address and I felt like somebody had punched me in the stomach.

---

Let me put the numbers on the table, because I know you and I know you'll want to talk about money, and I want there to be no confusion about any of it.

- Papa bought the building in 1979. Three floors on rue Saint-Hubert: the bakery on the ground, two apartments above.
- Since maman died in February, the building has been half yours and half mine. The estate was settled in August.
- I pay $2,400 a month in rent to the estate. I have never been late. Not once. Not one bounced cheque, not one phone call asking me for a favour, not one month where I had to explain myself.
- In 2019 I paid **$38,000** for the new roof on that building. My money, my signature, my decision. I did it because the roof was on the building and the building was on the bakery. If the agent tells you the roof is "solid" or "recently replaced" — that's me. That's my money sitting inside that $1,150,000.
- And you know the offer I made you. **In September, by phone**, I told you I wanted to buy your half. The caisse had already pre-approved me for $410,000. I told you that myself, on the phone, like a man making an offer to his brother. I never asked you for the whole building. I asked for your half, so the building could stay whole, so I could keep working in it, and so you could take your money and do whatever you want with yours.

Do you remember what you said to me when I told you that?

Because I remember.

---

Now let me tell you what happens next, because I have seen this play out on my street and I know how the story ends.

Somebody comes along with money. The three-storey on Saint-Hubert gets gutted, or it becomes six condos with a glass lobby and a doorman. The rent on the ground floor doubles. Maybe triples. The bakery is gone. The sign comes down. There is a nice new boutique where I used to bake at four in the morning.

You know what that means for me. I'm 57 years old. I have **six employees** who depend on this place — Karine, and the others, real people whose mortgages I have watched get paid. I have clients who have been buying their bread here since before you were in Calgary. Their mothers bought it before them. Some of them now bring their grandchildren on Saturday. A condo lobby does not need a baker, Denis. And I can't just go find another street with a lease that runs to **April 30, 2027** and a mortgage on a building I'm not going to be able to buy. I won't survive it. I'm not exaggerating for effect — I'm telling you exactly what is happening to me.

You think I'm sentimental. Fine. Let's be business about it for one minute, since you like that word better than I do.

Sentiment is thirty-one years, six jobs, thirty-one years of clients.

Business is this: the ground floor has been a working bakery every single day since 1994. The building has a roof because I paid for it. And the buyer for your half is standing right here, already approved, who is not going to keep making you offers while you shop around. If you sell to a developer, you get your money and I get an eviction letter and a broken back. That's not a good deal for the family. That's a bad deal for everybody, including you.

---

And Denis... I'm not going to pretend I don't remember certain things.

You were maybe seven, maybe eight. Papa let you sleep in the back room, in the flour sacks, because you asked him, and to you it was the greatest thing in the world. You told everybody it smelled like bread, that it was like being inside the oven without the heat. I remember him checking on you in the middle of the night. I remember you in that room with the light off, talking about nothing, the way kids do when they can't sleep.

I'm not telling you this to make you feel guilty. I'm telling you because *you* know what that building is. It is not a listing. It is not a line item with three bathrooms and a garage on Centris. It is the room where you slept. It is where I learned to work. It is where maman and papa lived and raised us and where our whole family started.

I don't want to lose my brother over this. I want to be clear about that. I'm not writing to destroy you. I'm writing because I couldn't sleep, because I kept thinking — I must be wrong, maybe I heard it wrong, maybe the agent got confused. But I saw Centris. It's real. And nobody called me.

---

So here is what I'm asking. Two things.

**1. Take the building off the market. This week.** Call your agent and pull the listing. I'm not asking you to give me your half for nothing. I'm asking you to stop the machine for a few days while we talk like brothers, on the phone, the way we should have done in September.

**2. If you truly don't want to sell to me at all, then give me the droit de premier refus.** Let me match any offer. Let me have the chance to buy your half before you sign anything with anybody. That's all. That's the whole request.

And I want to hear from you **by phone**. Not your wife, not by text, not a message I have to read between two loaves with flour on my hands. Call me. I don't care what time it is where you are. If it's three in the morning in Calgary, call me anyway — I'll pick up. I will be angry, but I'll listen.

I'd rather hear one sentence from you than a thousand words from a lawyer.

---

I love you, Denis. Even now, even angry, especially now. You're my little brother who slept in the flour sacks and thought it was the best room in the world. Don't test how much of that I can take.

Call me.

[Your first name]

---

A couple of practical things, since you asked me to help: keep a copy of this email, and if he doesn't call you within a few days, send it again with one line at the top — *"You have not called me, so I am writing again."* Don't add insults; the document is stronger without them. And if he says no to both asks, the "droit de premier refus" question is worth taking to your notary — in Quebec you can sometimes negotiate that into a co-ownership agreement even after the estate is settled, and a lawyer's letter costs less than losing the building.
